title: Service Discovery
description: How services find the network locations of healthy instances of other services as they scale and redeploy.

sections.overview: In a dynamic environment, instances come and go. Service discovery keeps a registry of healthy instances and lets callers resolve a logical name (orders-service) to current addresses.
sections.context: Discovery becomes necessary as soon as services call each other and instances change addresses. It is either client-side (the caller queries a registry and load-balances) or server-side (the caller hits a stable address such as a load balancer or cluster DNS name).
whenToUse: Any system of multiple services with autoscaling or rolling deploys.
whenNotToUse: A monolith behind one load balancer does not need a discovery system.
alternatives: Cloud load balancers with stable DNS names.
Service mesh, which bundles discovery with traffic policy.
failureModes: Stale registrations routing traffic to dead instances.
DNS caching beyond TTL in clients.
The registry itself becoming a single point of failure.
implementation: Use health checks tied to readiness, not just process liveness.
Respect DNS TTLs in client libraries.
Run the registry highly available, or use the platform's built-in mechanism.
sections.summary: Needed once services talk to each other; prefer the mechanism your platform already provides.

relations.note: Kubernetes provides orchestration and built-in service discovery, which is why discovery needs often lead teams to it.
A standalone registry and discovery system.
Meshes combine discovery with traffic policy.
A non-redundant registry can take down all service-to-service traffic.

title: API Gateway
description: A single entry point for API clients that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting and API lifecycle concerns.

sections.overview: An API gateway sits between clients and backend services. It routes requests, enforces authentication and authorization, applies rate limits and quotas, transforms protocols and collects API analytics.
sections.context: Gateways matter once there are many backend services or external consumers. They centralize cross-cutting concerns so each service does not reimplement them. Ingress handles cluster routing; a gateway handles API management.
whenToUse: Many services exposed to external clients.
Public or partner APIs needing keys, quotas and versioning.
whenNotToUse: A single service behind a load balancer.
When the gateway would hold business logic; keep it thin.
alternatives: Reverse proxy (NGINX, Envoy) with minimal policy.
Service mesh for internal traffic only.
failureModes: The gateway as a single point of failure or bottleneck.
Business logic creeping into gateway plugins.
sections.summary: Centralize edge concerns in a thin, redundant gateway.

relations.note: Once traffic fans out from a gateway to many services, you need observability to see what happens to each request.
Commonly used as a reverse proxy or gateway.
Data plane of several gateways.
All external traffic passes through it.
Rate limiting at the edge protects backends from bursts.

title: NGINX
description: A high-performance web server, reverse proxy and load balancer, also widely used as a Kubernetes ingress controller.

sections.overview: NGINX is an event-driven server used for static content, reverse proxying, TLS termination, load balancing and caching.
sections.context: It typically sits at the edge of an application tier or cluster, between a cloud load balancer and application processes.
whenToUse: Simple L7 load balancing and caching.
whenNotToUse: Dynamic configuration at large scale is easier with API-driven proxies such as Envoy.

relations.note: Can act as a basic gateway with routing and rate limiting.
A common ingress controller.
Overlapping proxy roles.

title: Envoy
description: A cloud-native L4/L7 proxy with API-driven configuration, used in service meshes and API gateways.

sections.overview: Envoy is a proxy designed for service-oriented architectures. Its configuration can be updated dynamically through xDS APIs, and it exposes detailed telemetry.
sections.context: Envoy is the data plane for several service meshes and gateways, so it often appears indirectly.
whenNotToUse: Configuring Envoy directly is complex; most teams use it through a control plane.
sections.summary: The building block behind many meshes and gateways.

relations.note: Data plane for several meshes.
Basis for several gateways.
Supports outlier detection and connection limits.

title: Consul
description: HashiCorp's service registry, health checking and service networking tool.

sections.overview: Consul maintains a catalog of services with health checks and exposes it through DNS and HTTP APIs. It also offers a service mesh and key-value configuration.
sections.context: Useful for discovery across mixed environments (VMs, multiple clusters) where Kubernetes DNS alone does not reach.
whenToUse: Discovery across VMs and multiple platforms.
whenNotToUse: Inside a single Kubernetes cluster, built-in discovery is usually enough.

relations.note: A dedicated registry and health-checking system.
Overlaps with Kubernetes' built-in discovery inside clusters.

title: CDN vs No CDN
description: Whether to put a content delivery network in front of your origin, and what to cache at the edge.
question: Should we put a CDN in front of our application?
problems: my site is slow for users far away
how can I reduce cloud costs

sections.overview: A CDN caches content at points of presence near users and proxies the rest to your origin. Modern CDNs also provide TLS termination, DDoS protection, WAF and edge compute.
sections.context: For most public web applications a CDN improves latency, reduces origin load and egress cost, and adds protection. The main design work is deciding what is cacheable and how to invalidate it.
whenToUse: Public web content and static assets.
Origins that need protection from traffic spikes and attacks.
whenNotToUse: Highly personalized, uncacheable APIs where the only benefit would be TLS termination (still often worth it for protection).
sections.cost: CDN egress is often cheaper than cloud origin egress, and offloaded requests reduce origin compute.
failureModes: Caching personalized responses and leaking data between users.
Mass invalidation or cache expiry sending a thundering herd to the origin.
The CDN provider itself as a dependency; configuration pushes can have global impact.
sections.summary: Use a CDN for public web traffic by default. Be deliberate about cache keys, invalidation and what happens when the CDN misbehaves.

values: CDN fees; lower origin egress and compute
Absorbs spikes; adds a provider dependency
DDoS mitigation and WAF at the edge

relations.note: Request collapsing at the edge reduces origin stampedes.
A single CDN provider becomes a dependency for all traffic.
A case study of a large CDN and edge network.
Offloading traffic lowers cost per request.

title: L4 vs L7 Load Balancing
description: Comparing connection-level (TCP/UDP) load balancing with request-level (HTTP) load balancing.
question: Do we need request-aware (L7) load balancing, or is connection-level (L4) enough?

sections.overview: L4 load balancers forward TCP/UDP connections without inspecting content. L7 load balancers parse HTTP and can route by host, path or header, terminate TLS and balance individual requests.
whenToUse: L4: non-HTTP protocols, very high throughput, static IPs, minimal latency.
L7: HTTP routing, TLS termination, gRPC/HTTP/2 request-level balancing.
whenNotToUse: L4 balances connections, so long-lived HTTP/2 connections can pin load to a few backends.
L7 adds processing cost and is another component that inspects traffic.
sections.summary: Use L7 for HTTP applications and L4 for raw throughput or non-HTTP traffic.

values: Rules, certificates, health checks per route

relations.note: Can act as an L7 load balancer.
Load distribution is how horizontal scaling works.
